```ts
    builtin?: boolean;
    /** Where it was installed from. */
    source?: PackageSource | null;
    /** Its data directory. */
    dataDirectory?: string | null;
  }[];
  /** Every `packages.setEnabled` / `uninstall` / `install`, newest last. */
  readonly packageCalls: {
    /** Which call. */
    method: "setEnabled" | "uninstall" | "install";
    /** The target plugin id. */
    id: string;
    /** `setEnabled`'s value. */
    enabled?: boolean;
    /** `uninstall`'s `removeData` option. */
    removeData?: boolean;
    /** `install`'s source (`{ kind: "file" }` when not given). */
    source?: PackageSource;
    /** `install`'s `replace` option. */
    replace?: boolean;
  }[];
  /**
   * Packages `validate` and `validateArchive` accept: path (directory or `.vxp` file) → its manifest. Other paths fail with `missing`. `install` adds or upgrades the entry in TestHost.packages following the player's source rules: the same source upgrades, another source needs `replace` (`conflict` otherwise), a built-in id is `unsupported`.
   */
  readonly candidates: Map<string, PackageManifest>;
  /**
   * Remote Markdown images (`plugin.ui.markdown`): address → a local PNG or JPEG file served for it, or `null` for a failing download. Nothing is fetched from the network in tests; unknown addresses fail.
   */
  readonly remoteImages: Map<string, string | null>;
  /**
   * The Markdown document a value holds (its wire form read back), or `null` when the value is not one. `images` maps each remote address to the downloaded file. Pass a whole property value or a field of one: a document nested in rows is read the same way.
   */
  markdown(value: Json | undefined): MarkdownWire | null;
  /** What `player.audioDevices()` lists. `setAudioDevice` updates `host.source.audioOutput`. */
  audioDevices: {
    /** The device id, e.g. `coreaudio/<UID>`. */
    id: string;
    /** The system's name for it. */
    name: string;
  }[];
  /** Replace the plugin list and push `packages.changed` (another plugin started, stopped, was installed or removed). */
  setPackages(list: TestHost["packages"]): void;
  /**
   * Simulate another plugin calling `player.next()` / `previous()`: the host asks this plugin's sequence provider. Rejects with `unavailable` when there is no provider or its flag is false.
   */
  step(direction: "next" | "previous"): Promise<unknown>;
  /** The plugin's command with this local id. Throws when it is not registered (never added, or disposed). */
  command(id: string): FakeCommand;
  /**
   * The plugin's tool window with this id (by default the file name without extension: `ui/picture.slint` → `picture`). Throws when it was never opened with `show()`.
   */
  window(id: string): FakeWindow;
  /**
   * The plugin's mounted panel (bottom bar, sidebar or backdrop). Throws when none is mounted. Its `props` use Slint (kebab-case) names; `emit` fires a callback on the panel's global.
   */
  mounted(): Omit<FakeWindow, "callbacks" | "userClose"> & {
    /** `"bottom"`, `"sidebar"` or `"backdrop"`. */
    slot: string;
    /** The exported component the SDK found in the file. */
    component: string;
    /** The last `panel.setInteraction(...)` locks, `null` before any. */
    locks: Json;
  };
  /** The parameters of every request of one wire method, oldest first. */
  sent(method: string): Record<string, Json>[];
  /**
   * Wait until no request is in flight (and the SDK's follow-up passes ran),
   * and at least `ms` milliseconds have passed so that timers due by then
   * fired. Call it after every action that makes the plugin talk to the host,
   * before asserting.
   *
   * It only waits for host calls. Work the plugin does on its own (reading
   * or parsing a file, a child process, a network request) is not waited
   * for: on a loaded machine it can finish after `settle()` returns. Poll
   * the result you assert on instead (second example).
   * @param ms - Extra time to wait, for debounces and timers (default 0).
   */
  settle(ms?: number): Promise<void>;
  /** Close the fake stream servers and delete the host's temporary directories. `stop()` from startPlugin calls it. */
  close(): void;
}
```

### startPlugin

Activate a plugin against a test host, the way the player's runner does:
build the `plugin` object, call `activate(plugin)`, wait for every
registration started during activation (commands, panels, resolvers, ...),
then wait until the host is idle.

The manifest id and capabilities come from `directory/manifest.json`
unless `capabilities` is given; then `id` (default `"test.plugin"`) and
`capabilities` are used and no manifest is read. Calls that need an
undeclared capability fail with `capability`, as in the player.

Rejects when `manifest.json` cannot be read or parsed, when `activate`
throws, or when a registration made during activation fails (for example
`limit`, `conflict`, `invalid`), which is when the player would fail the
activation.

- @param activate - The plugin's default-exported `activate` function.
- @param options - Where the plugin lives and how to start it.
- @returns `host`: the TestHost; `plugin`: the object passed to `activate` (call the plugin API on it directly); `stop()`: dispose the plugin like the player stopping it (scopes released, stores flushed), wait until the host is idle and remove the host's temporary files.

```ts
function startPlugin(activate: (plugin: Plugin) => unknown, options?: {
  /**
   * The plugin's package directory, as a path or a `file:` URL (e.g. `new URL("..", import.meta.url)` from `tests/`). Relative `.slint` files resolve against it. Default: the current working directory.
   */
  directory?: string | URL;
  /** The manifest id when `capabilities` is given. Default `"test.plugin"`. */
  id?: string;
  /** Use these capabilities instead of reading `manifest.json`. */
  capabilities?: string[];
  /** A host to use (to preset data before activation). Default: a new one. */
  host?: TestHost;
  /** Use an existing directory as `plugin.dataDirectory` (to test a restart). */
  dataDirectory?: string;
  /**
   * The interface language to play (TestHost.locale): the plugin's `locales/<locale>.po` (or `.json`) in `directory` is loaded and its menus, messages and titles show translated. Default: the host's.
   */
  locale?: Locale;
}): Promise<{
  /** The test host the plugin talks to. */
  host: TestHost;
  /** The `plugin` object passed to `activate`. */
  plugin: Plugin;
  /** Stop the plugin, wait for the host, and remove temporary files. */
  stop(): Promise<void>;
}>;
```

### COMMAND_LIMITS

The player's command registry caps, the same values as the player's own
table (the player's tests check that they agree). They are runaway guards,
not product limits: a command added past them fails with code `limit`
(its `ready` rejects; during activation, activation fails), commands
already registered are unaffected, and disposing a command frees its slot
at once. TestHost enforces the same caps.

For menus built from media content (tracks, chapters, presets), set your
own sensible display cap well below `perPlugin`.

```ts
const COMMAND_LIMITS: {
  /** Commands one plugin instance may have at the same time (160). */
  readonly perPlugin: 160;
  /** Commands of every plugin plus the player's own, together (1024). */
  readonly total: 1024;
};
```

### MENU_IDS

The player's built-in top-level menus, by id. Write `@<id>` as the first
segment of a command path (`["@video", "Blur"]`, see `CommandOptions.path`) to put a
command into that menu whatever language the player's menus are in. The
player stores the menu's title (视频 today); later segments are titles.
Needs player 0.3.0 (`"minPlayerVersion": "0.3.0"`); older players show
`@video` as a menu of its own. The player's tests check that this list
agrees with the player's.

```ts
const MENU_IDS: readonly ["open", "playback", "subtitles", "video", "audio", "screen", "settings"];
```

### LOCALES

The player's interface languages: English (the source language) first,
then the translations, as the player's own table (its tests check that
they agree).

```ts
const LOCALES: readonly ["en", "zh-Hans", "ja", "ko", "de", "fr", "es"];
```

### LIST_SEPARATORS

The separator of each list style per interface language, as the player's
table (`i18n::text::SEPARATORS`; its tests check that they agree).

```ts
const LIST_SEPARATORS: Readonly<Record<Locale, Readonly<Record<ListStyle, string>>>>;
```

### TEXT_LIMITS

The player's limits on one text value (a
Text or
TextList with everything nested in it), as the player's
`i18n::text` (its tests check that they agree).

```ts
const TEXT_LIMITS: {
  /** Nesting depth of texts and lists; the value itself is depth 0 (8). */
  readonly depth: 8;
  /** Texts, lists and arguments in all, the value itself included (1024). */
  readonly nodes: 1024;
  /** Arguments of one text (16). */
  readonly args: 16;
  /** Items of one list (256). */
  readonly items: 256;
  /** UTF-8 bytes of a source text or a string argument (4096). */
  readonly stringBytes: 4096;
};
```

### UI_VALUE_LIMITS

The player's limits on one property value (a `PropValue` as written
by `View.set` or `View.bind`, or an initial property of a
window, panel or settings page). The player's tests check that these
agree with the player; TestHost enforces them the same way.

A value over a limit is refused whole with code `limit` (the property
keeps what it showed) and reported to `Scope.onError`: a write by
`View.set` or `View.bind` as described there. As an initial property it
makes `Window.show` reject; a panel or settings page opens without it and
the failure goes to the plugin's `onError`.

They bound the work one write costs the player's interface thread; they
are not meant as list sizes to aim for. A list that can grow without
bound (a playlist, a history) should send the rows near the view and say
how many there are, not the whole list.

```ts
const UI_VALUE_LIMITS: {
  /** Nesting depth; the value itself is depth 0 (8). */
  readonly depth: 8;
  /** Values in all, counting every array, object, string, number, boolean and null, the value itself included; a Markdown document is one (16384). */
  readonly values: 16384;
  /** Rows of one array (4096). */
  readonly arrayRows: 4096;
  /** UTF-8 bytes of one string or object field name (64 KiB). */
  readonly stringBytes: number;
  /** UTF-8 bytes of all strings and field names together, the text of the value's Markdown documents included (1 MiB). */
  readonly textBytes: number;
};
```

### HostError

A definite refusal from the player (or the plugin runner), with a stable
`code`. Plugin code sees it as a `PluginError` (an `Error` with `code`);
branch on `code`, never on `message`.

In tests, throw one from a TestHost.handle override to simulate the
player refusing a request: the SDK treats it exactly like a real refusal
(the call rejects with that `code`, nothing is retried). Throwing a plain
`Error` instead simulates a lost reply, which makes the SDK run its
recovery path (asking the host about the operation again).

Common codes: `stale` (the condition no longer holds; nothing was done),
`invalid` (bad argument), `missing` (unknown target), `capability`
(undeclared capability), `busy`, `conflict`, `unavailable`, `unsupported`
(refused, not executed), `backend` (load or parse failure), `failed`,
`timeout`, `aborted`, `limit` (a player limit such as the command count),
`disabled` (the plugin is stopping).

```ts
class HostError extends Error {
  /** The stable error code, e.g. `"invalid"`, `"stale"`, `"unavailable"`. */
  code: string;
  /**
   * @param code - The stable error code the caller will see as `error.code`.
   * @param message - Human-readable detail (not for branching on).
   */
  constructor(code: string, message: string);
}
```

## Internal types the API refers to

Not exported (do not import them); listed because public declarations use them.

### Filter

```ts
interface Filter<T> extends Disposable {
  /**
   * Desired chain; last write wins. An empty chain (video `[]`; audio `nodes: []` with no delay) removes this chain, leaving other chains alone; nothing is sent if it was never applied. Players before 0.3.0 refuse an empty video chain with `invalid`.
   */
  set(value: T): void;
  /** Current status. */
  readonly status: FilterStatus;
  /** The status changed. */
  onStatus(listener: (status: FilterStatus) => void): Disposable;
  /** Re-check the host and apply the current value again. */
  retry(): void;
}
```

### MediaJob

```ts
type MediaJob = {
  jobId: number;

    libavfilterVersion: string;

      start: number;
      end: number | null;

      containerStartTime: number | null;
      expectedContainerStartTime: number;
    };
    nativeSubtitle?: {
      codec: "subrip" | "srt";
      streamIndex: number;
      canonical: {
        format: "srt";

      };
    };

  outcome: null | {
    destination: string;
  } | {

    };

  };
};
```

```ts
  local?: LocalServices;
  /** The interface language of this run (`plugin.i18n.locale`): the runner passes the player's `VESTRA_LOCALE`, the test host its `locale`. */
```

### PlaybackStats

What Player.stats reports. Every field is the backend's own value
(libmpv properties), `null` when it has none; nothing is converted.

```ts
interface PlaybackStats {
  /**
   * The rendering path: "libmpv · GPU 渲染（OpenGL）" (GPU, macOS default) or "libmpv · 软件渲染" (software: Windows, Linux, headless, fallback). The strings are the player's display text.
   */
  backend: string;
  /** The playback session number. */
  session: number;
  /** Frames the host has shown. */
  framesShown: number;
  /** Frames dropped, `null` when unknown. */
  framesDropped: number | null;
  /** Every field is the backend's own value, `null` when it has none. */
  video: {
    /** Codec name. */
    codec: string | null;
    /** Coded width. */
    width: number | null;
    /** Coded height. */
    height: number | null;
    /** Frames per second (after a `frameBlend` node: the output rate). */
    fps: number | null;
    /** Short decoder name, e.g. "h264". */
    decoder: string | null;
    /** e.g. "yuv420p". */
    pixelFormat: string | null;
    /** Colour matrix, e.g. "bt.709". */
    colorspace: string | null;
    /** Size after aspect correction and filters. */
    displayWidth: number | null;
    /** Size after aspect correction and filters. */
    displayHeight: number | null;
    /** Measured display refresh; only with display-synced output (usually null). */
    displayFps: number | null;
    /** Bits per second, updated per keyframe. */
    bitrate: number | null;
    /** Hardware decoder in use, e.g. "videotoolbox"; "no" = software decoding. */
    hwdec: string | null;
    /** Transfer characteristic as mpv names it, e.g. "bt.1886", "pq", "hlg". */
    transfer: string | null;
  } | null;
  /** `null` without audio. */
  audio: {
    /** Codec name. */
    codec: string | null;
    /** Hz. */
    sampleRate: number | null;
    /** Channel count. */
    channels: number | null;
    /** Short decoder name, e.g. "aac". */
    decoder: string | null;
    /** Sample format, e.g. "floatp". */
    format: string | null;
    /** Readable layout, e.g. "stereo", "5.1(side)". */
    channelLayout: string | null;
    /** Bits per second. */
    bitrate: number | null;
  } | null;
  /** Last audio/video difference in milliseconds (signed). */
  avSyncMs: number | null;
  /** Seconds of media buffered ahead by the demuxer. */
  cacheSeconds: number | null;
```

```ts
type CommandDeclaration = {
```

## Examples

Complete Vestra Player plugins, each with a manifest, its source, Slint files, tests and a README. CI checks, tests and packs every one of them against the SDK in this repository. The [Examples](https://vestrasys.github.io/vestra-player-sdk/documents/Examples.html) page of the documentation lists them with their walkthroughs.

Run one (the SDK is linked from this repository, so build it first):

```sh
npm ci                      # in the repository root
cd examples/hello
npm install
npm run check && npm test && npm run pack
```

Each example is laid out the same way: `manifest.json` (id `examples.<name>`), `main.ts`, `ui/*.slint`, `tests/*.test.ts`, `package.json` (depends on `"@vestra-player/sdk": "file:../.."`), `README.md`. To start your own plugin from one, copy its folder and change the dependency to `"@vestra-player/sdk": "^1.5.0"` and the manifest `id`.

### Example: hello

The [Quick start](https://github.com/vestrasys/vestra-player-sdk#quick-start), runnable: one menu command, **Tools → Hello**, that shows an on-screen message.

| Capabilities | API |
| --- | --- |
| `commands`, `ui.osd` | `commands.add`, `osd.show`; tests with `startPlugin` |

#### Walkthrough

The smallest useful plugin: one menu command that shows a message over the video. It is the README's Quick start as a runnable project.

#### The manifest

(code: `manifest.json`, below)

- `id` names the plugin, as `<owner>.<name>` (your GitHub user or organization). `vestra.` ids are reserved for the player's built-in plugins.
- `entry` is the module the player loads: the TypeScript file itself during development.
- `capabilities` lists what the plugin may do. `commands` lets it add a menu command, `ui.osd` lets it show a message over the video. A call without its capability fails with `code: "capability"`.

#### The code

(code: `main.ts`, below)

From top to bottom:

1. `import type` brings in the SDK's types only. The player creates the `plugin` object, so the built plugin contains none of the SDK's code.
2. The default export, `activate`, is what the player calls when it loads the plugin.
3. plugin.commands.add registers a command. `id` is its name inside the plugin; `path` puts it in the main menu, and the last segment is the label.
4. `run` is called when the user picks the item. plugin.osd.show shows the message. Returning its promise lets the SDK report a failure instead of losing it.

Nothing needs cleaning up: the command belongs to `plugin` and is removed when the plugin stops.

#### The test

(code: `tests/main.test.ts`, below)

- startPlugin runs `activate` against TestHost, an in-memory player. `directory` makes it read `manifest.json`, so the test has the plugin's real capabilities.
- `host.command("hello")` is the registered command: its `declaration` (here the menu path) and `run()`, which acts like a click.
- `host.osd` lists every message the plugin showed.

#### Try next

1. **A shortcut.** Add `bindings: ["Ctrl+Alt+H"]` to the command; the key then runs it too.
2. **A different menu.** Use `path: ["@playback", "Hello"]` to join the player's own **Playback** menu, and add `"minPlayerVersion": "0.3.0"` to the manifest (menu ids are new in 0.3.0).
3. **Go further.** Getting started adds a window and state; Bookmark is the next example.

#### examples/hello/manifest.json

```json
{ "id": "examples.hello", "version": "0.1.0", "apiVersion": "vestra/1", "entry": "main.ts", "capabilities": ["commands", "ui.osd"] }
```

#### examples/hello/main.ts

```ts
import type { Plugin } from "@vestra-player/sdk";

export default async function activate(plugin: Plugin) {
  plugin.commands.add({
    id: "hello",
    path: ["Tools", "Hello"],
    run: () => plugin.osd.show("Hello"),
  });
}
```

#### examples/hello/tests/main.test.ts

```ts
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import test from "node:test";
import { startPlugin } from "@vestra-player/sdk/testing";
import activate from "../main.ts";

test("Tools → Hello shows an on-screen message", async () => {
  const { host, stop } = await startPlugin(activate, {
    directory: new URL("..", import.meta.url), // reads manifest.json
  });
  const hello = host.command("hello");
  assert.deepEqual("path" in hello.declaration && hello.declaration.path, [
    "Tools",
    "Hello",
  ]);
  await hello.run();
  assert.deepEqual(host.osd, ["Hello"]);
  await stop();
});
```

### Example: blur

A live Gaussian blur over the video that is playing. **Video ▸ Blur…** opens a small window with one slider: move it to blur the video, set it to 0 to turn the blur off.

| Capabilities                                                           | API                                                                                                                                      |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `commands`, `ui.window`, `processing.video`, `playback.read`, `events` | `commands.add` in the `@video` menu, `windows.create` with `bind` and `on`, `video.filter` with a `gblur` node; tests with `startPlugin` |

#### Walkthrough

This walkthrough builds **Blur**: a menu command opens a small window with one slider, and the slider blurs the video that is playing. It is about 40 lines of TypeScript and 40 lines of Slint, and it shows three parts of the API working together: a command, a tool window and a video filter.

The complete source is in [`examples/blur/`](https://github.com/vestrasys/vestra-player-sdk/tree/main/examples/blur). Every code block on this page is taken from those files, so it is always the code CI checks and tests.

#### The manifest

(code: `manifest.json`, below)

A call whose capability is missing from the manifest fails with `code: "capability"`. Blur needs five:

| Capability                | Why                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `commands`                | `plugin.commands.add`: the menu item.                                                                                                                                                 |
| `ui.window`               | `plugin.windows.create`: the Blur window.                                                                                                                                             |
| `processing.video`        | `plugin.video.filter`: the blur itself.                                                                                                                                               |
| `playback.read`, `events` | A filter reads the player's state, and follows its changes, to know when there is a video to apply the blur to. Without `events` a blur set before a video starts would stay waiting. |

`minPlayerVersion` is 0.3.0 because the menu path uses the `@video` menu id and the window uses `Theme.danger`, both new in that version. Older players refuse to load the plugin with a clear message.

#### main.ts, top to bottom

##### Activation

(code: `main.ts`, part "activate", below)

The SDK is imported with `import type` only: the player passes the `plugin` object to `activate`, and everything the plugin creates through it (the filter, the window, the command) is released when the plugin stops. There is no cleanup code to write.

##### The filter

(code: `main.ts`, part "filter", below)

- `plugin.video.filter("blur")` creates this plugin's **filter chain**, a list of processing nodes the player runs on every decoded frame. Creating it sends nothing.
- `strength` is the plugin's only state. The window shows it and the slider changes it.
- `Math.round(value * 10) / 10` keeps one decimal. The window's label shows one decimal too, and a slider dragged all the way left lands on exactly 0 instead of 0.02.
- `{ kind: "gblur", sigma, steps: 3 }` is FFmpeg's Gaussian blur. `sigma` is the radius, 0–10 (the slider's range); `steps` must be 3. A value out of range would be refused with `invalid`.
- `[]` is the empty chain: it removes this plugin's blur and leaves other plugins' filters alone.
- `blur.set(chain)` returns immediately. The SDK applies the chain when a video plays and again for every new video, so the plugin calls `set` only when the strength changes.

**Calling `set` on every mouse move is fine.** While you drag, the window reports a new value dozens of times a second. The filter sends at most one request at a time; a `set` while a request is on its way only replaces the pending value, so the player always ends up with the latest value and never works through a queue of old ones.

##### The window

(code: `main.ts`, part "window", below)

- `plugin.windows.create("ui/blur.slint")` loads the window file but does not open it. The window's id is the file name, `blur`.
- `bind(() => ({ … }))` keeps the window's properties equal to what the function returns. The SDK calls it again after every callback and every change of the filter's status, and sends only the values that changed. The plugin never pushes updates by hand.
- `blur.status` is `waiting`, `applying`, `applied` or `failed`. Only a failure is worth showing here, with the player's reason in `error.message`. One failure you can see on purpose: a **generated stream** (such as the signal generator) does not pass through the player's filters, so while one plays the status is `failed` with the code `unsupported`. The blur comes back by itself when a video plays again.
- `on("strengthChanged", setStrength)` connects the Slint callback `strength-changed` to the function above. TypeScript may use either spelling.

##### The command

(code: `main.ts`, part "command", below)

- `path: ["@video", "Blur…"]` puts the item in the player's own **Video** menu. Menu paths are matched by their exact titles, and the player's menus are titled in its own language, so `["Video", "Blur…"]` would create a second top-level menu. A first segment that starts with `@` names a built-in menu whatever its title. The built-in menu stays where it is, and an item without `order` goes at the end of it.
- `run` opens the window, or shows it again after the user closed it. Returning the promise of `show()` lets the SDK report a failure to the plugin log.

#### ui/blur.slint

(code: `ui/blur.slint`, below)

- The imports come from the player at run time: `Theme` holds its colours and sizes, so the window follows the player's colour scheme, and `Slider` looks like the player's own sliders.
- A window file exports one component that inherits `Window`.
- **Properties carry data from the plugin to the window.** `strength` is `in-out` because the user changes it too; `problem` is `in` because only the plugin writes it.
- **Callbacks carry actions from the window to the plugin.** `strength-changed` passes the slider's new value.
- `value <=> root.strength` is a **two-way binding**. A one-way binding (`value: root.strength`) would be broken by Slint the first time the user drags the slider, and from then on the plugin could no longer move it, for example when the window is opened again.
- `changed(value)` fires on every mouse move during a drag: that is what makes the blur follow the slider live.
- The label rounds the value to one decimal, like `setStrength`.

#### The tests

(code: `tests/blur.test.ts`, below)

`startPlugin` runs `activate` against `TestHost`, an in-memory player that speaks the real protocol, so the SDK's filter logic runs unchanged; there is no video and no Slint. `host.setSource({ phase: "ready" })` pretends a video is playing, `window.emit` fires a Slint callback as if the user had moved the slider, and `host.processing.resources` holds what the player currently applies for each plugin. Always `await host.settle()` before checking: it waits until every request has been answered.

#### Try next

1. **Remember the strength.** Keep it in `plugin.storage.json("blur", { defaults: { strength: 0 } })`, call `save` in `setStrength`, and call `setStrength(store.value.strength)` at activation. See `Storage`.
2. **A shortcut and a check mark.** Add a second command with `bindings: ["Ctrl+Shift+B"]` that switches between 0 and the last strength, and `checked: () => strength > 0` so the menu shows whether the blur is on. See `CommandOptions`.
3. **Presets.** Add a `ComboBox` with Light, Medium and Strong to the window and a callback that calls `setStrength` with 2, 5 or 9. Because `strength` is bound two-way, the slider moves with it.

#### examples/blur/manifest.json

```json
{
  "id": "examples.blur",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "apiVersion": "vestra/1",
  "entry": "main.ts",
  "minPlayerVersion": "0.3.0",
  "capabilities": [
    "commands",
    "ui.window",
    "processing.video",
    "playback.read",
    "events"
  ],
  "name": "Blur",
  "author": "Vestra Player SDK examples",
  "punchline": "A live Gaussian blur over the video that is playing",
  "description": "Video ▸ Blur… opens a small window with one slider: move it to blur the video, set it to 0 to turn the blur off.\nSDK example: a menu command, a tool window and a video filter.",
  "tags": ["video", "filter", "blur", "example"]
}
```

#### examples/blur/main.ts

```ts
/**
 * Blur: Video ▸ Blur… opens a window with one slider that blurs the video.
 * Walkthrough: docs/examples/blur.md.
 */
import type { Plugin, VideoNode } from "@vestra-player/sdk";

export default function activate(plugin: Plugin) {
  // This plugin's video filter chain; nothing is sent until set().
  const blur = plugin.video.filter("blur");
  let strength = 0; // the Gaussian sigma, 0–10; 0 means off

  function setStrength(value: number) {
    strength = Math.round(value * 10) / 10; // one decimal, like the label
    const chain: VideoNode[] =
      strength === 0 ? [] : [{ kind: "gblur", sigma: strength, steps: 3 }];
    blur.set(chain);
  }

  const window = plugin.windows.create("ui/blur.slint");
  window.bind(() => ({
    strength,
    // Empty unless the player refused the blur.
    problem: blur.status.state === "failed" ? blur.status.error.message : "",
  }));
  window.on("strengthChanged", setStrength);

  plugin.commands.add({
    id: "blur",
    path: ["@video", "Blur…"], // the player's Video menu, in any language
    run: () => window.show(),
  });
}
```

#### examples/blur/ui/blur.slint

```slint
// The Blur window: one slider. Walkthrough: docs/examples/blur.md.
import { Theme } from "@vestra/theme.slint";
import { Slider } from "@vestra/widgets.slint";

export component BlurWindow inherits Window {
    title: "Blur";
    width: 280px;
    background: Theme.bg-panel;

    in-out property <float> strength;
    in property <string> problem;
    callback strength-changed(float);

    VerticalLayout {
        padding: Theme.dialog-padding;
        spacing: 8px;
        HorizontalLayout {
            spacing: 8px;
            Slider {
                minimum: 0;
                maximum: 10;
                value <=> root.strength;
                changed(value) => { root.strength-changed(value); }
            }
            Text {
                width: 24px;
                text: round(root.strength * 10) / 10;
                color: Theme.text;
                font-size: Theme.font-body;
                horizontal-alignment: right;
            }
        }
        Text {
            text: root.problem;
            color: Theme.danger;
            font-size: Theme.font-body;
            wrap: word-wrap;
        }
    }
}
```

#### examples/blur/tests/blur.test.ts

```ts
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import test from "node:test";
import { startPlugin, TestHost } from "@vestra-player/sdk/testing";
import activate from "../main.ts";

/** Start the plugin with a video already playing. */
async function start() {
  const host = new TestHost();
  host.setSource({ phase: "ready", duration: 60 });
  return startPlugin(activate, {
    directory: new URL("..", import.meta.url), // reads manifest.json
    host,
  });
}

/** The video chain the player holds for this plugin (`[]` when there is none). */
function chain(host: TestHost) {
  const [resource] = host.processing.resources.values();
  return resource?.nodes ?? [];
}

test("Video ▸ Blur… opens the window; the slider blurs the video", async () => {
  const { host, stop } = await start();
  const command = host.command("blur");
  assert.deepEqual("path" in command.declaration && command.declaration.path, [
    "@video",
    "Blur…",
  ]);
  await command.run();
  const window = host.window("blur");
  assert.equal(window.visible, true);

  window.emit("strength-changed", 4);
  await host.settle();
  assert.deepEqual(chain(host), [{ kind: "gblur", sigma: 4, steps: 3 }]);
  assert.equal(window.props["problem"], "");
  await stop();
});

test("strength 0 removes the blur", async () => {
  const { host, stop } = await start();
  await host.command("blur").run();
  const window = host.window("blur");
  window.emit("strength-changed", 6.5);
  await host.settle();
  window.emit("strength-changed", 0.02); // rounds to 0
  await host.settle();
  assert.deepEqual(chain(host), []);
  assert.equal(host.processing.resources.size, 0);
  await stop();
});

test("stopping the plugin withdraws the blur", async () => {
  const { host, stop } = await start();
  await host.command("blur").run();
  host.window("blur").emit("strength-changed", 3);
  await host.settle();
  assert.equal(host.processing.resources.size, 1);
  await stop();
  assert.equal(host.processing.resources.size, 0);
});
```

### Example: signal-generator

A plugin that generates its own video and audio: **Open ▸ Signal generator** plays colour bars with a 1 kHz sine tone, and choosing it again stops them.

| Capabilities | API |
| --- | --- |
| `commands`, `producer.av`, `playback.control`, `playback.read` | `player.openStream` with a `frame()` callback, `Stream.stop` and `onStop`, a checkable command in the `@open` menu; tests with `startPlugin` |

#### Walkthrough

This walkthrough builds a plugin that **generates its own video and audio** and plays them in Vestra Player like any other source: colour bars and a 1 kHz sine tone. It is about 110 lines of TypeScript in one file, with no window. Along the way it covers how Player.openStream pulls frames from a plugin, how a frame's pixels are laid out, how many audio samples go with each picture, how to keep a tone smooth across frames, and how to stop a stream.

The complete, tested source is in [`examples/signal-generator`](https://github.com/vestrasys/vestra-player-sdk/tree/main/examples/signal-generator). Every code block on this page is taken from those files, so it always matches the code that CI checks and tests.

#### How a generated source works

Usually the player plays a file: it decodes the picture and the sound and keeps them in step. A **generated source** has no file. The plugin calls `openStream` with a frame size and a `frame()` function, and the player plays whatever `frame()` returns. To the user it is a source like any other: it replaces what was playing, play/pause works, and opening a file replaces it in turn.

The plugin does not push frames on a timer of its own. **The player pulls them:** the SDK calls `frame()` whenever the player needs more.

- `frame()` is never called twice at the same time, and not at all while the player is paused.
- It is paced by the **audio clock**. The SDK keeps a little audio queued ahead of the sound card (about 50 ms) and calls `frame()` when the queue runs low.
- It is **synchronous**: it cannot `await`, so everything it needs must already be in memory. If it is slow, the sound drops out.

Each call returns one picture and **the audio that plays while that picture is on screen**. The stream's timeline is its audio: the player plays the samples at 48 000 per second and shows each picture when the audio reaches it. A frame that carries 1600 samples therefore lasts 1600 / 48 000 s = 1/30 s. The number of samples per frame _is_ the frame rate; there is no separate setting.

#### The manifest

(code: `manifest.json`, below)

| Capability         | Why                                                                                                                                                                           |
| ------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `commands`         | The menu command.                                                                                                                                                             |
| `producer.av`      | `player.openStream`: producing frames.                                                                                                                                        |
| `playback.control` | The stream becomes the player's source, like opening a file, and Stop closes it. `openStream` needs this as well as `producer.av`.                                            |
| `playback.read`    | When it stops, the stream reads the player's state to check that it is still the current source before closing it, so it never closes a file the user opened in the meantime. |

`minPlayerVersion` is 0.3.0 because the command's path uses the `@open` menu id, new in that version. The display fields (`name`, `punchline`, `description`, …) are what the plugin manager and the store show.

#### main.ts, top to bottom

##### The format

(code: `main.ts`, part "format", below)

- 640×360 is plenty for a test picture: the player scales it to the window. A frame may be at most 4 MiB, so 1280×720 is the largest 16:9 size.
- `FPS` is 29.97, the NTSC rate, on purpose: 48 000 / 29.97 = 1601.6 samples is not a whole number, which is the interesting case (see frame()). At 25 or 30 fps the division is exact.
- A stream's audio is always 48 kHz, stereo, 32-bit float; the plugin cannot choose another rate.
- `LEVEL` is the tone's amplitude. Samples must stay within −1…1: a sample outside that range, or one that is not a number, ends the stream with the code `invalid`.

##### The picture: RGBA bytes

(code: `main.ts`, part "bars", below)

A frame's picture is a `Uint8Array` of exactly `width × height × 4` bytes: **red, green, blue and alpha for each pixel, row by row, starting at the top left**. So pixel (x, y) starts at byte `(y × width + x) × 4`:

- `x * 7 / WIDTH` picks the bar: the first 1/7 of every row is grey, the last 1/7 blue.
- The values are 75 % (191 of 255), as in the classic SMPTE test bars.
- Alpha 255 means opaque. The player shows the picture as it is.

The bars never change, so they are drawn once when the module loads.

##### frame()

(code: `main.ts`, part "frame", below)

This is the function the player calls for every frame. Three things happen in it.

**How many samples.** 48 000 / 29.97 = 1601.6. Rounding every frame down to 1601 would make the sound run 0.6 samples short per frame, about 1.3 seconds per hour, and the picture would drift away from it. Instead, `owed` accumulates the exact amount, the frame takes the whole samples, and the fraction is carried to the next frame:

| Frame | `owed` before | Samples | Carried |
| ----- | ------------- | ------- | ------- |
| 0     | 1601.6        | 1601    | 0.6     |
| 1     | 1602.2        | 1602    | 0.2     |
| 2     | 1601.8        | 1601    | 0.8     |
| 3     | 1602.4        | 1602    | 0.4     |

The frames alternate between 1601 and 1602 samples, and the total never differs from the exact time by more than one sample, however long the stream runs.

**The sine, phase-continuous.** The obvious formula, `sin(2π × frequency × t)`, needs the time `t`, and it makes every frame start the wave from scratch unless `t` is tracked exactly. Instead the code keeps a **phase**: the position inside the current cycle, from 0 up to (not including) 1.

- The sample is `LEVEL × sin(2π × phase)`.
- After each sample, the phase advances by `FREQUENCY / SAMPLE_RATE`: at 1 kHz that is 1/48 of a cycle, so a cycle takes 48 samples.
- At 1 the phase wraps back to 0, so the number never grows and never loses precision.

`phase` lives outside `frame()`, so each frame continues exactly where the previous one ended. That matters: a frame of 1601.6 samples holds 33.37 cycles, not a whole number, so a wave restarted at every frame would jump, and a jump in a waveform is heard as a click, 30 times a second. With the phase it is one smooth tone. The same trick keeps the tone smooth when the frequency changes (see Try next).

**Interleaved stereo.** The audio is one `Float32Array` with the channels alternating: `audio[2 * i]` is the left sample of sample frame `i`, `audio[2 * i + 1]` the right one. Its length is twice the number of samples.

**Reusing the buffers.** `frame()` returns the same `video` array every time, and `audio` is a view into one buffer allocated up front, big enough for the longest frame (1602 stereo samples). That is safe: the SDK copies each frame before it calls `frame()` again. Allocating new arrays 30 times a second would work too, but it gives the garbage collector work, and a long collection pause is heard as a dropout.

##### Starting and stopping

(code: `main.ts`, part "start-stop", below)

- `openStream({ width, height, frame })` resolves once the stream plays. Before that, the SDK has set up a local connection to the player, called `frame()` a few times to fill the first buffers, and asked the player to make the stream its source. It rejects if that fails, for example with `device` when the audio output is not ready, or `timeout` after 10 seconds; the error then goes to the plugin log.
- `starting` covers the moment between the call and its result, so that choosing the command twice quickly does not start two streams.
- `onStop` is called when the stream ends **without** the plugin stopping it: the user opened a file, or the stream failed (its argument is then the error). The plugin just forgets the stream, and the menu's check mark goes away. It is not called for the plugin's own `stop()`.
- `stop()` forgets the stream first, then calls `stream.stop()`. That closes the source if it is still the player's source, then the frame connection, then the producer. In that order the player sees an ordinary "closed" source rather than a playback failure. If another source already replaced the stream, `stop()` leaves that source alone.

When the plugin is disabled or the player quits, the SDK stops the stream the same way: it belongs to `plugin`.

##### The command

(code: `main.ts`, part "command", below)

- `path: ["@open", "Signal generator"]` puts the item in the player's own **Open** menu. Menu paths are matched by their exact titles, and the player's menus are titled in its own language, so `["Open", …]` would add a second top-level menu. A first segment starting with `@` names a built-in menu whatever its title.
- `checked` is a function. The SDK calls it again after every handler and every `onStop`, and updates the check mark when the result changes.
- `run` starts the stream when there is none and stops it when there is one. It returns the promise so that a failure reaches the plugin log.

#### The tests

(code: `tests/signal-generator.test.ts`, below)

- The first two tests call `frame()` directly, with no player: the picture's size and colours, the 1601/1602 sample counts and their total, and that no step between two neighbouring samples is larger than a clean 1 kHz sine allows, across frame boundaries too.
- The third runs the plugin against `TestHost`, the SDK's in-memory player. It speaks the real protocol, including the frame connection, so the SDK's start-up and stop sequence run unchanged. `host.producers.get(1)` is the player's end of the stream: `released` says the plugin let go of it, and `droppedWhileSelected` would be `true` if the connection had closed while the stream was still the player's source.
- A stream runs on timers, so the test polls with `until()` instead of relying on `host.settle()`.

#### Try next

1. **A frequency slider.** Add a tool window with one `Slider` (see Blur) and make `FREQUENCY` a variable that its callback changes. The next `frame()` uses the new value; because the phase continues, the pitch glides without a click.
2. **Movement.** Draw a white bar whose position depends on a frame counter. A dropped or repeated frame then shows as a jump.
3. **Show why it stopped.** Add the `ui.osd` capability and call `plugin.osd.show(error.message)` in `onStop` when `error` is not `null`.

```json
{

  "version": "1.0.0",
  "apiVersion": "vestra/1",
  "entry": "main.ts",
  "minPlayerVersion": "0.3.0",
  "capabilities": [
    "commands",
    "producer.av",
    "playback.control",
    "playback.read"
  ],
  "name": "Signal Generator",
  "author": "Vestra Player SDK examples",
  "punchline": "Colour bars and a 1 kHz test tone generated by a plugin",
  "description": "Open ▸ Signal generator plays colour bars with a 1 kHz sine tone that the plugin generates itself. Choose it again to stop.\nSDK example: Player.openStream.",
  "tags": ["example", "test signal", "audio", "video"],
  "sourceUrl": "https://github.com/vestrasys/vestra-player-sdk/tree/main/examples/signal-generator",
  "license": "Apache-2.0"
```
